_comment: Test Twin Propeller Aircraft (TTPA) requirements for IHW3a, the SIZING loop. This file REPLACES Ttpa_requirements_IHW2.json for IHW3a: read this one and only this one. It carries the aerodynamics, propulsion, constraints and missions blocks of IHW2 forward so the mission analysis of IHW1 and the constraint analysis of IHW2 run against it unchanged, and it adds the three things a sizing loop needs that neither earlier homework had: a real geometry block (wing planform, tail volume coefficients, fuselage layout, nacelle), a weights block (Raymer Table 15.2 component build-up), and a sizing block (guess, tolerance, relaxation).
_what_changed_from_IHW2: Three things that were FIXED in IHW1/IHW2 are now OUTPUTS of the loop. (1) W_TO was 5354 lbf, the converged answer of the IHW1 mission analysis, typed into the IHW2 driver by hand. (2) S_ref and P_SL were computed ONCE from that W_TO and the design point. (3) OEW came from the statistical regression 0.911*W_TO^0.947, so it depended on nothing but weight. In IHW3a the geometry is rebuilt from W_TO on every iteration, OEW is built up from that geometry, CD0 follows the wetted area, the mission fuel follows CD0, and the takeoff weight closes on all of it.
_who_reads_what: geometry -> TtpaGeom and TtpaAero constructors. aerodynamics -> TtpaAero. propulsion -> TtpaProp. weights -> TtpaWeights. sizing -> the run_ttpa_sizing driver and sizing_loop. constraints.conditions -> ConstraintSetImporter.read_conditions, then get_con. constraints.design_point -> solve_design_point. missions -> MissionProfileReader.read_profile, then get_miss_seg and run_mission.

geometry._comment: EXTENDED IN IHW3a. In IHW1 and IHW2 this block held one number, the aspect ratio, because neither homework had any real geometry: TtpaGeom carried S_ref = NaN and S_wet = NaN. The sizing loop has to rebuild the airplane from W_TO on every iteration, so the planform shape, the tail volume coefficients, the fuselage layout and the nacelle all live here now. Read by the TtpaGeom constructor; TtpaAero still reads AR from this block, exactly as it did in IHW2.
geometry._what_is_an_input_here: Only SHAPE lives in this block - ratios, angles and the fixed cabin-driven fuselage. SIZE does not: S_ref is written by the sizing loop from W_TO and the wing loading, and every span, chord, area and wetted area is a Dependent property of TtpaGeom recomputed from S_ref on every read. No derived quantity is stored here or in the class.
geometry._src_AR: Carried over from IHW1/IHW2. Preliminary wing aspect-ratio design assumption.
geometry._src_taper_ratio: Raymer Sec. 4.3.3: an unswept wing normally takes a taper ratio near 0.4. Corroborated by Roskam Part II, Table 6.3.
geometry._src_sweep_quarter_chord_deg: The airplane cruises near M = 0.3, so no sweep is needed. Raymer Fig. 4.2, Roskam Part II Table 6.3. Carried for reporting; the sizing loop does not read it.
geometry._src_thickness_ratio: NACA 23018 at the root and NACA 23009 at the tip, Roskam Part II Table 8.3. The MEAN of the two is what Raymer Eq. 7.12 needs to turn exposed planform area into wetted area; the ROOT value is what the Torenbeek wing-fuel-volume equation needs.
geometry._src_twist_incidence_dihedral: Raymer Sec. 4.3.4 (-3 deg washout for stall behaviour), Sec. 4.3.5 (2 deg incidence), Table 4.2 with Roskam Part II Table 6.3 (5 deg dihedral). Reporting only - none of the three enters the sizing loop.

horizontal_tail._src: Volume coefficient and moment arm from Roskam Part II Table 8.3(a). CORROBORATED BY TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES: Raymer Table 6.4 prints 0.80 for a general-aviation twin engine - an exact match - and Nicolai and Carichner Table 11.1 reports 0.64 to 1.07 across fourteen twin light reciprocating-propeller airplanes. Planform from Roskam Part II Table 8.13. NACA 0012 airfoil, hence t/c = 0.12. Equation: S_ht = V_h * S_ref * MAC / arm [Raymer Eq. 6.29, p. 159]. The area is THEORETICAL, carried to the aircraft centreline, which is the convention the method is defined in. The tail GROWS with the wing on every iteration - one of the two couplings the sizing loop exists to capture.

vertical_tail._src: Volume coefficient and moment arm from Roskam Part II Table 8.3(b). CORROBORATED: Raymer Table 6.4 prints 0.07 for a general-aviation twin engine, and the 0.065 used here sits inside the 0.045 to 0.080 band of Nicolai and Carichner Table 11.1 for the same class. Planform from Roskam Part II Table 8.13, NACA 0012. Equation: S_vt = V_v * S_ref * b / arm [Raymer Eq. 6.28, p. 159]. Note the length scale is the wing SPAN, not the MAC - that is the only difference between the two tail-volume definitions.

fuselage._comment: The fuselage is CABIN-DRIVEN, not weight-driven: two-abreast seating, three rows, six occupants. It therefore does NOT change during the sizing loop, which is what keeps the loop well behaved - the fuselage contributes a constant to the empty weight and to the wetted area while the wing and the tails grow. Every length below is fixed by the cabin layout and by the two fineness ratios, not by W_TO.
fuselage._src_width_height: Cabin width 4.75 ft (two 1.75 ft seats plus a 1.25 ft aisle, Roskam Part III Table 3.1 and Raymer Table 9.1) plus 1.5 in of structural depth per side gives a 5.0 ft fuselage width. Cabin height 5 ft plus a floor allowance gives 5.75 ft, which is also the maximum fuselage diameter l_d.
fuselage._src_lengths: Total fuselage length 31.6 ft = 5.5 * l_d, the fuselage fineness ratio of Roskam Part II Table 4.1 / Part III Fig. 3.1. Tail cone 14.4 ft = 2.5 * l_d, the aft-body fineness ratio of Roskam Part II Table 4.1 / Part III Fig. 3.3. Constant section 9.0 ft = three rows at a 3 ft seat pitch (Roskam Part III Sec. 3.3.2.2). The nose is the remainder, 31.6 - 14.4 - 9.0 = 8.2 ft. The three lengths must sum to 31.6 ft; TtpaGeom checks that.
fuselage._src_tailcone_end: Closure dimensions at the aft end of the tail cone. Raymer Eq. 7.13 works from the projected top and side areas, and a cone taken to a point understates both. A 10 deg upsweep over a 14.4 ft cone does not close completely.

nacelle._comment: Wing-mounted tractor nacelles, one per engine. The nacelle LENGTH tracks the engine, which grows with P_SL, so the nacelle wetted area is inside the sizing loop. The nacelle DIAMETER does not: Raymer Table 10.3 states that the width and the height of an opposed piston engine vary insignificantly over a +50 percent power change, so a fixed diameter is the right model here.
nacelle._src_diameter_ft: Raymer Table 10.4, horizontally-opposed column: engine width 2.6-2.8 ft. The upper end is taken so the cowl encloses the engine and its cooling plenum.
nacelle._src_length_over_engine_length: Layout assumption, NOT a textbook value. The nacelle runs from the spinner bulkhead to the aft cowl fairing and so is longer than the bare engine that Raymer Table 10.4 sizes. A factor of 2.0 reproduces the roughly 7 ft nacelle of a light twin of this class. It is the weakest number in this block: change it and the parasite drag moves.

landing_gear._comment: Tricycle gear. These two ratios convert the converged takeoff weight into the static loads the struts and tyres are sized to. They are used AFTER the loop converges, not inside it - the gear WEIGHT inside the loop is the Raymer Table 15.2 fraction of W_TO.
landing_gear._src: Raymer Ch. 11: the static load on the main gear is W * l_n/l_d and on the nose gear is W * l_m/l_d, where l_d is the nose-to-main wheelbase, l_n the aft-cg-to-nose-gear distance and l_m the forward-cg-to-main-gear distance. Until a weight-and-balance study fixes the cg envelope, 0.90 and 0.15 are the standard placeholders.

aerodynamics._comment: Carried over from IHW2, with ONE addition and ONE change of role. The addition is Cfe. The change is CD0_clean: it is no longer the model, it is the CROSS-CHECK. In IHW2 the clean CD0 was a fixed 0.028 read straight out of this file. In IHW3a the airplane has real geometry, so TtpaAero computes the clean CD0 from the wetted area instead, and CD0_clean stays here as the IHW2 value to compare against. Everything else in this block - the three CLmax values, the stall margin, the flap, gear and propeller increments - is unchanged and is still read exactly the same way.
aerodynamics._how_the_configuration_polar_is_built: CD0_config = CD0_clean + the flap increment + the gear increment (+ the stopped-propeller increment in the engine-out climb). e_config = e_clean + the flap increment, where e_clean is still computed from the aspect ratio inside TtpaAero. K1_config = 1/(pi*AR*e_config). CLmax_config is read directly from the three CLmax keys below.
aerodynamics._src_CD0_clean: Clean (cruise) zero-lift drag coefficient. Same value that was hardcoded in the IHW1 TtpaAero; it now comes from this file so that there is exactly one place to change it.
aerodynamics._role_of_CD0_clean_in_IHW3a: REFERENCE VALUE, not a model input. TtpaAero.CD0 is a Dependent property computed from the geometry with Raymer Eq. 12.23. The run script prints both; they agree to about one percent, and that agreement is the check that the geometry and the wetted-area build-up are right.
aerodynamics._src_Cfe: NEW IN IHW3a. Raymer Table 12.3, equivalent skin-friction coefficient for a light TWIN-engine airplane (the single-engine row is 0.0055). Used with Raymer Eq. 12.23, CD0 = Cfe * S_wet / S_ref, to get the clean zero-lift drag of the airplane the loop has just laid out. This is the single equation that couples GEOMETRY to DRAG, and therefore to mission fuel and to takeoff weight.
aerodynamics._src_CLmax: Roskam Part I, Table 3.1 (twin-engine propeller-driven, FAR 23): clean 1.2-1.8, takeoff 1.4-2.0, landing 1.6-2.6. Mid-range values assumed for the TTPA. Pull the one that matches the configuration of the condition you are evaluating: clean for the engine-out climb, takeoff for the takeoff ground roll and the all-engines climb, landing for the landing ground roll and the balked landing.
aerodynamics._src_CL_stall_margin: Roskam Part I, Sec. 3.3. The steepest climb is flown near CLmax, which is unsafe because the airplane is then close to the stall, so the climb lift coefficient is taken 0.2 below the CLmax of that configuration. Apply it inside get_config_polar so that no constraint function can forget it.
aerodynamics._src_delta_CD0: Roskam Part I, Table 3.6, zero-lift drag increments: takeoff flaps 0.010-0.020, landing flaps 0.055-0.075, landing gear extended 0.015-0.025. Mid-range values assumed. The gear increment adds on top of the flap increment when the gear is down.
aerodynamics._src_delta_e: Roskam Part I, Table 3.6, Oswald-efficiency increments: about -0.05 with takeoff flaps and about -0.10 with landing flaps. Extending the gear does not change e.
aerodynamics._src_delta_CD0_propeller_stopped: Roskam Part I, Sec. 3.3: drag increment of the stopped propeller of the failed engine. Add it only when the condition sets propeller_stopped, which is the one-engine-inoperative climb.

propulsion._comment: Carried over from IHW2 with the engine-size regression added. IHW2 needed to know how much power the engine MAKES; the sizing loop also needs to know how much it WEIGHS and how long it is, because the first feeds the empty weight and the second feeds the nacelle wetted area, and both follow from P_SL - one of the two states the loop iterates on.
propulsion._src_n_engines: NEW. Twin-engine airplane. In the one-engine-inoperative climb only 1 of the 2 engines is running, so the available power is divided by this number.
propulsion._src_BSFC: Carried over from IHW1. Preliminary brake-specific fuel consumption of the piston engine, used by the cruise and loiter mission segments.
propulsion._src_eta_p_mission: Carried over from IHW1. Propeller efficiencies of the cruise and loiter mission segments.
propulsion._src_eta_p_climb: NEW. Propeller efficiency in a climb. The climb-gradient constraint needs it, and the mission analysis never did, because IHW1 modelled climb with a fixed weight fraction.
propulsion._src_P_TO_over_P_max_continuous: NEW. Roskam Part I, Sec. 3.3: for a typical piston engine the takeoff power is about 1.1 times the maximum continuous power. The all-engines climb must be flown at maximum continuous power, so the power available there is the takeoff power divided by this number.
propulsion._src_engine_regression: NEW IN IHW3a. Raymer Table 10.4, British block, horizontally-opposed piston column: W_engine = 5.47 * bhp^0.780 [lb] and L_engine = 0.32 * bhp^0.424 [ft], both PER ENGINE, with bhp the rated power of ONE engine. Horizontally-opposed is the right column: Raymer Sec. 10.5 notes that opposed engines now dominate general aviation. Divide P_SL by n_engines before using these.
propulsion._src_bhp_range_of_validity: Raymer Table 10.4 prints 60-500 bhp as the applicable range of the opposed-engine regression. TtpaProp warns, and does not error, when the loop asks for a per-engine power outside it: an intermediate iterate can leave the band and come back.

weights._comment: NEW IN IHW3a. In IHW1 and IHW2 the empty weight was one line inside TtpaWeights, OEW = 0.911 * W_TO^0.947, and the payload was a literal 1200. That regression knows only the takeoff weight: build a bigger wing or hang a bigger engine on the same airplane and it returns the same answer. A sizing loop needs an empty weight that RESPONDS to the airplane it has just laid out, so IHW3a replaces it with the Raymer Table 15.2 component build-up. The old regression is kept below as a cross-check and is reported next to the build-up.
weights._the_buildup: OEW = wing + horizontal tail + vertical tail + fuselage + landing gear + installed engines + all-else-empty. The first four are an areal density times an area; the last three are fractions. Raymer Table 15.2, General Aviation column throughout.
weights._src_W_payload: Carried over from IHW1. One pilot and five passengers at 200 lb each, including baggage. This is the number the whole closure is solved for: everything else is a fraction of W_TO, and the payload is what those fractions have to leave room for.
weights._src_unit_weights: Raymer Table 15.2, General Aviation column. The wing and the two tails multiply EXPOSED PLANFORM area; the fuselage multiplies WETTED area. Mixing those two multipliers up is the classic error with this table - the fuselage row is the only wetted one.
weights._src_landing_gear_fraction: Raymer Table 15.2, General Aviation, times TOGW. The table footnote splits it 15 percent nose and 85 percent main, and says to subtract 0.014*W_0 for fixed gear. The TTPA retracts, so the full 0.057 applies.
weights._src_installed_engine_factor: Raymer Table 15.2, General Aviation, times the BARE ENGINE WEIGHT of all engines. Note that the GA column is 1.4, not the 1.3 of the fighter and transport columns. It covers the mount, the cowl, the exhaust, the starter and the rest of the installation. The bare engine weight comes from the Table 10.4 regression in the propulsion block.
weights._src_all_else_empty_fraction: Raymer Table 15.2, General Aviation, times TOGW. Covers flight controls, instruments, hydraulics, electrics, avionics, air conditioning and furnishings in one term. The GA column is 0.1; the fighter and transport columns are 0.17.
weights._src_statistical_OEW: The IHW1 empty-weight regression, OEW = 0.911 * W_TO^0.947, from the Nicolai light-propeller-airplane trend. KEPT AS A CROSS-CHECK ONLY. TtpaWeights.OEW now returns the component build-up; TtpaWeights.OEW_statistical returns this, and the run script prints both. They should agree within a few percent. If they do not, the geometry is wrong.
weights._src_fuel_density_lb_per_ft3: BACK-DERIVED, NOT AN INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT. The course wing-layout notebook states that a 37 ft^3 wing holds 1770 lb of 100LL 'at low temperature', and 1770/37 = 47.8 lb/ft^3. That value is adopted here so the fuel-volume check reproduces the course number. For reference, 100LL at 15 degC is about 6.0 lb/US gal = 44.9 lb/ft^3, which would give 1562 lb of capacity instead of 1663 lb - still far above the roughly 1019 lb the mission needs, so the conclusion of the check does not depend on which figure is used. Used only AFTER the loop converges.
weights._src_method: 'table_15_2' is the Raymer Table 15.2 areal-density build-up - the lecture's 'Empty weight II'. 'raymer_ga_III' is the lecture's 'Empty weight III': the same build-up with TWO rows replaced by the Raymer Sec. 15.3.3 general-aviation statistical equations. WHY IT EXISTS: Table 15.2's wing row is an areal density times area, so it contains NO aspect ratio. The lecture shows the consequence directly - an aspect-ratio trade study run on that model concludes that more aspect ratio is always better, which is wrong, and only a wing weight that carries AR produces the real structures-against-aerodynamics minimum. Use 'raymer_ga_III' for any AR trade study.
weights._rows_replaced_by_raymer_ga_III: WING -> Raymer Eq. 15.46, which carries (A/cos^2 Lambda)^0.6, so aspect ratio finally has a weight penalty. INSTALLED ENGINE -> Raymer Eq. 15.52, W = 2.575*W_en^0.922*N_en, which INCLUDES THE PROPELLER AND THE ENGINE MOUNTS. The Table 15.2 factor of 1.4 does not model a propeller at all, so the current build-up is missing that weight entirely. The other five rows stay at Table 15.2: swapping them would need a dozen new inputs (strut lengths, tank counts, avionics weight) for a few percent, and the lecture's point is specifically about the wing.
weights._src_ultimate_load_factor: N_z = 1.5 x the limit load factor. 14 CFR 23 normal category sets the limit at n = 2.1 + 24000/(W_TO + 10000), capped at 3.8; at 5100 lbf that formula gives 3.69, and the cap value 3.8 is taken as the design case, so N_z = 5.7. Read only by the Raymer Sec. 15.3.3 equations of method 'raymer_ga_III'.

_src_design_range_nmi: Design mission range 1,200 nmi. Fixed payload assumes single pilot crew and 5 additional passengers assumed to be 200 lb each.

sizing._comment: NEW IN IHW3a. Everything the sizing loop needs that is not a property of the airplane: where to start, when to stop, and how hard to damp each step. Read by run_ttpa_sizing and passed into sizing_loop. No discipline class reads this block.
sizing._the_framework: IHW3a follows the PRELIMINARY DESIGN FRAMEWORK of the sizing-refinement lecture. In that framework S_ref is a green INPUT - a design variable you choose - and the wing loading is a COMPUTED quantity, W_0/S_ref. The design diagram is then read at that ONE wing loading to get the power the requirements demand, and two red loops close the airplane: the MTOW iteration on W_0 and the T_0 iteration on P_0. The lecture states the consequence outright: you do not need to draw the whole matching chart, because W/S is fixed. That is what mode 'fixed_wing_area' does, and it is what makes the trade studies in run_ttpa_trade_studies possible.
sizing._src_mode: 'fixed_wing_area' is the lecture framework: S_ref below is the design variable, W/S = W_0/S_ref is computed, and the design diagram supplies the binding power loading at that single W/S. 'design_point' is the IHW2 route kept for continuity: the matching diagram is solved for a design point and S_ref = W_0/(W/S) becomes an OUTPUT. The framework's own SizingLoopL2, which the F-16 and 777 examples drive, is the 'design_point' form - it is the special case of the lecture framework in which S_ref happens to land on the envelope corner. Run both.
sizing._src_S_ref_ft2: THE DESIGN VARIABLE of mode 'fixed_wing_area'. Read by the loop, not by any discipline: the loop writes it into the geometry every iteration. The default is the wing the 'design_point' mode converges to, so the two modes can be compared directly. Sweep it with run_ttpa_trade_studies to see the objective move.
sizing._src_W_TO_guess_lbf: The same starting guess IHW1 used. The loop reaches the same answer from anywhere between about 2500 and 10000 lbf, so this is a convenience, not an input to the answer. Change it and check that nothing moves: that is the test that the fixed point is real.
sizing._src_design_point_mode: Either 'selected' or 'optimum'. 'selected' holds the design point at constraints.design_point, the (40, 9.25) chosen in IHW2 with a factor of safety, and checks its feasibility on every iteration. 'optimum' re-solves the matching envelope on every iteration and sizes to the least-engine corner instead. Run both: the difference between the two answers is the price of the margin.
sizing._src_tol_max_iter: Relative tolerance on BOTH states. The loop stops only when |W_TO_new - W_TO|/W_TO_new and |P_SL_new - P_SL|/P_SL_new are both below tol_rel. 1e-6 is the same test the metabook TOGW algorithm uses. Convergence takes about 30 iterations from the default guess, so 200 is a generous ceiling.
sizing._src_relaxation: Under-relaxation factors in (0,1] for the two states: x <- x + w*(x_new - x). Numerical damping, not physics, and NOT optional here. A full step (w = 1) taken from a guess far from the answer overshoots into the region where the empty and fuel fractions consume the whole takeoff weight; the closure denominator goes negative and the loop stops with a closureInfeasible error. At w = 0.5 it converges from every guess between 2500 and 10000 lbf.
sizing._src_relaxation_fixed_wing_area: Relaxation for BOTH states in mode 'fixed_wing_area', which needs a different value from the design-point mode. The reason is a real difference in the coupling. With the design point fixed, the power loading is a constant and P_0 just tracks W_0. With the wing area fixed, a heavier airplane means a higher W/S, which the takeoff constraint answers with a LOWER allowed W/P, which means a bigger and heavier engine, which means a heavier airplane - a loop that overshoots and rings. At 0.5 it converges in about 110 iterations with a visible oscillation; at 0.40 it takes about 60. Measured, not guessed.

constraints._comment: NEW IN IHW2. The requirements the matching diagram is built from. Read the conditions with ConstraintSetImporter.read_conditions(json_path), which returns a 1x6 struct array in the order below; get_con then pulls one of them out. Each condition holds REQUIREMENT data only: where the airplane is, in what configuration, at what weight and power, and what it must achieve there. No CLmax, no CD0, no propeller efficiency and no power lapse appears here - all of those come from your TtpaAero and TtpaProp objects at run time.
constraints._note_missing_keys: The six conditions do not all carry the same keys: a field-length condition has distance_ft, a climb condition has G, the cruise condition has ktas and power_index. Where a key is absent the importer leaves an empty value ([]), so read the optional keys through a helper that returns a default. The defaults are beta = 1.0, power_setting = 1.0, config = clean, and false for the three logical flags.
constraints._note_beta: beta = W_condition / W_TO, the weight at which the condition must be met, referred to takeoff weight. It is a SPECIFIED REQUIREMENT INPUT, not an output of your mission analysis. beta = 0.975 is the weight after startup, taxi, takeoff and the initial climb: Roskam Part I Table 2.2 gives 0.984 for startup/taxi/takeoff and 0.990 for climb, and 0.984 x 0.990 = 0.974, which is the same pair of fractions your IHW1 run_mission applies. It represents an airplane that loses an engine or returns to the field soon after takeoff.
constraints._note_power_setting: power_setting is the throttle fraction of the rated power at that condition (1.0 = full power). The altitude power lapse, the maximum-continuous derate and the one-engine-inoperative split are NOT stored here: your TtpaProp applies them from n_engines, P_TO_over_P_max_continuous and the flags on the condition.
constraints._note_config: config names the flap and landing-gear position. The five names your get_config_polar must accept are clean, takeoff_flaps_gear_up, takeoff_flaps_gear_down, landing_flaps_gear_up and landing_flaps_gear_down. They are the names the framework uses in AerodynamicsBase.get_config_polar.
constraints._src_wing_loading_range_psf: Wing-loading sweep of the matching diagram, lbf/ft^2, and the number of points on it. Read by the driver script, not by any constraint function: every constraint function receives the sweep as its first argument.

design_point._comment: The design point SELECTED from the matching diagram. It is a design decision, not a result. The analysis finds the corner of the feasible region, which is the smallest engine the requirements permit and which sits exactly on two constraints with no margin at all; the designer then backs away from that corner. Read by the driver script.
design_point._src: Design point read off the matching diagram, kept clear of the least-engine corner as a factor of safety on the preliminary sizing.

conditions.name: Takeoff
conditions._src: Takeoff ground roll of 1,500 ft at sea level, and the climb to 50 ft above the takeoff surface of 14 CFR 23.2115. Sized with the FAR 23 takeoff parameter, Roskam Part I Sec. 3.1: S_TGR = 4.9 TOP23 + 0.009 TOP23^2, with TOP23 = (W/S)(W/P) / (sigma CLmax_TO). beta = 1.0 because takeoff happens at takeoff weight by definition.

conditions.name: Landing
conditions._src: Landing ground roll of 1,500 ft at sea level after a 50-ft obstacle, 14 CFR 23.2130. Sized with Roskam Part I Sec. 3.2: S_LGR = 0.265 Vs_L^2, with S_LGR in ft and Vs_L in kt. This condition limits the wing loading only; it does not constrain the power loading.

conditions.name: Climb AEO
conditions._src: 14 CFR 23.2120 (Part 23 Level 2, low speed), all engines operating: minimum climb gradient of 8.3 % with the landing gear retracted, the flaps in the takeoff position and both engines at maximum continuous power. max_continuous = true is what makes your TtpaProp divide the available power by P_TO_over_P_max_continuous.

conditions.name: Climb OEI
conditions._src: 14 CFR 23.2120 (Part 23 Level 2, low speed), one engine inoperative: minimum climb gradient of 1.5 % at 5,000 ft with the landing gear and the flaps retracted and the remaining engine at takeoff power. oei = true divides the available power by n_engines; propeller_stopped = true adds the stopped-propeller drag increment of the failed engine.

conditions.name: Climb BL
conditions._src: 14 CFR 23.2120 (Part 23 Level 2, low speed), balked landing: minimum climb gradient of 3.0 % with the landing gear extended, the flaps in the landing position and both engines at takeoff power.

conditions.name: Cruise Speed
conditions._src: Minimum cruise speed of 200 KTAS at 8,000 ft. Sized with the power index of Roskam Part I Sec. 3.6, Ip = [ (W/S) / (sigma (W/P)) ]^(1/3), read from Fig. 3.28 at 200 kt as Ip = 1.4. The cruise power of a propeller-driven airplane is set to 80 % of the rated power, which is power_setting. No beta is given because the cruise weight cancels: it divides the wing loading and the power loading by the same factor. ktas is the requirement this condition came from and is carried for reporting; the analysis itself uses power_index.
conditions._src_method: 'power_index' is the Roskam Part I Sec. 3.6 correlation of IHW2: W/P <= (W/S)*kP/(sigma*Ip^3), read off Fig. 3.28 at Ip = 1.4. It does NOT read the drag polar, which is why the design point never moves as the geometry changes. 'drag_based' replaces the correlation with the actual power balance at the required speed: W/P <= 550*eta_p*kP/(beta*V*(C_D/C_L)), with C_L = beta*(W/S)/q from the airplane's own wing loading and C_D from its own polar. THE TWO DISAGREE MATERIALLY. On the sized airplane the correlation allows W/P <= 11.24 while the drag calculation demands W/P <= 8.67, which means the (40, 9.25) design point is about 6 percent short of 200 KTAS at the specified 80 percent power setting - it makes the speed at full throttle with 17 percent margin. Switching to 'drag_based' also makes the cruise constraint depend on C_D0 and K, so the design point genuinely moves during the sizing loop.

missions._comment: Carried over from IHW1 unchanged, so that your mission analysis runs against this file with no edit. Read with MissionProfileReader.read_profile(json_path, 'std_mission'), then one segment at a time with get_miss_seg. The constraint analysis needs the takeoff gross weight your mission analysis converges to.

std_mission._description: Standard design mission consisting of startup, taxi, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent, loiter, descent, and landing.
std_mission._cite_reserve_fuel_fraction: 6% reserve/trapped-fuel allowance applied on top of the complete mission.
std_mission._src_cruise: Cruise requirement: 1,200 nmi at 8,000 ft and 200 KTAS.
std_mission._src_loiter: 45-minute design loiter at 4,000 ft and 120 KTAS. Reserve fuel is applied separately on top of the full mission.
std_mission._src_method: 'L1' is the IHW1 mission: Roskam Table 2.2 fixed fractions everywhere, cruise and loiter by Breguet at L/D_max and 0.866*L/D_max. 'L2' is the IMPROVED FUEL FRACTIONS of the sizing-refinement lecture: the lift coefficient is computed from the ACTUAL wing loading at each condition, so the fuel finally responds to the wing. The lecture draws this as the W_0/S_ref arrow into the Fuel fraction box, and it is the largest single error in the L1 mission - see _why_L2_matters.
std_mission._why_L2_matters: On the sized airplane the L1 model uses L/D = 13.45 in cruise, but 200 KTAS at 8000 ft with a wing loading near 39 psf puts the airplane at C_L = 0.366, where the real L/D is 10.53. The model is 27.6 percent optimistic. Best-L/D speed for this airplane is 139 kt and the requirement is 200 kt, so it genuinely cruises well below best L/D. In loiter the error runs the other way: 120 KTAS at 4000 ft lands almost exactly on best L/D (C_L 0.774 against an optimum 0.758), so the 0.866 factor makes the L1 model 13.4 percent pessimistic there.
std_mission._src_cruise_segments: Number of sub-segments the cruise is broken into for the L2 mission. The lecture's rule is that no segment weight fraction may fall below 0.9; at 1200 nmi the whole-cruise fraction is about 0.84, so one segment is not enough. Twelve puts every sub-segment above 0.985 and the answer is converged to well under a pound against 40 segments.
std_mission._src_climb_segments: Sub-segments per climb for the L2 energy-method climb. Four is ample over an 8000 ft climb.
std_mission._src_ground_segment_method: Applies to the startup/taxi/takeoff block and to landing. 'roskam_fraction' keeps the Table 2.2 values (0.984 and 0.992). 'lecture_idle_rule' uses the lecture's 15 min at idle plus 1 min at takeoff power, with idle taken as 5 percent of maximum power. THE LECTURE RULE IS KEPT AS AN OPTION AND NOT THE DEFAULT, on purpose: it is written for a jet. Applied to this piston twin with a constant BSFC it predicts about 6.5 lbf for start, taxi and takeoff combined, against 82 lbf from Roskam, because a piston engine's specific fuel consumption at idle is far worse than at cruise and a constant-BSFC model cannot see that. The lecture itself says to use the idle fuel flow 'for your particular engine', which is data this model does not carry. Roskam's GA-calibrated fraction is the better answer here. The lecture makes the same call for descent and landing: the historical method is good enough.
std_mission._src_credit_climb_distance: The lecture allows the ground distance covered in the climb to be credited against the cruise range. Left OFF by default so the 1200 nmi cruise requirement means the same thing it did in IHW1 and IHW2. Turning it on shortens the cruise by roughly 8 nmi, which is inside the noise.
